steps.focus: Nhận biết am/is/are trong câu giới thiệu bản thân và đồng nghiệp
steps.usage: Dùng động từ to be để giới thiệu tên, vai trò và trạng thái trong cuộc họp nhóm. Chọn am với I, is với he/she/it (và danh từ số ít), are với you/we/they (và danh từ số nhiều).
steps.formula: I am / He is / She is / We are / They are + danh từ hoặc tính từ
examples: I am a software tester.
She is our project manager.
We are ready for the year-end review.
dailyObjectives: Ngày 1: Bước 1 – Nhận biết am/is/are trong tin nhắn giới thiệu thành viên nhóm.
Ngày 2: Bước 1 – Ghi nhớ cấu trúc khẳng định với am, is, are.

steps.focus: Phủ định isn't/aren't và câu hỏi Are you…? Is he…?
steps.usage: Dùng phủ định để nói điều không đúng về bản thân hoặc đồng nghiệp, và câu hỏi để xác nhận thông tin trong cuộc họp. Đảo to be lên trước chủ ngữ khi đặt câu hỏi.
steps.formula: I am not / He isn't / They aren't + …; Am I…? / Is he…? / Are you…?
examples: He isn't in the meeting today.
Are you the new team leader?
Is the report ready for Monday?
dailyObjectives: Ngày 3: Bước 2 – Hình thành phủ định isn't/aren't và câu hỏi Are you…? Is he…?
Ngày 4: Bước 2 – Dùng to be khi nói về thời điểm và tín hiệu nhận biết trong họp nhóm (today, now, this week).

steps.focus: Lỗi thường gặp với to be và trả lời ngắn
steps.usage: Người Việt thường quên to be vì tiếng Việt không dùng động từ này trong câu tương tự. Trả lời ngắn Yes, I am. / No, she isn't. giúp phản hồi nhanh trong họp.
steps.formula: Subject + am/is/are + (not) + thành phần; Yes, I am. / No, he isn't.
examples: Wrong: I a developer. → Right: I am a developer.
Wrong: Are you ready? Yes, I are. → Right: Yes, I am.
Wrong: She is not agree. → Right: She doesn't agree. (dùng to be đúng: She isn't sure.)
dailyObjectives: Ngày 5: Bước 3 – Sửa lỗi thiếu to be và dùng sai am/is/are.
Ngày 6: Bước 3 – Viết 1–2 câu giới thiệu bản thân và trả lời ngắn Yes, I am. về công việc của mình.

steps.focus: Nhận biết I/me/my/mine, he/him/his, they/them/their trong tin nhắn công việc
steps.usage: Đại từ làm chủ ngữ đứng trước động từ, còn my, his, their đứng trước danh từ để chỉ sở hữu. Dùng trong email và tin nhắn nhóm để nói về bản thân và đồng nghiệp.
steps.formula: I / he / they (chủ ngữ) + động từ; my / his / their + danh từ
examples: My report is almost done.
His team works on the mobile app.
Their meeting starts at 9 a.m.
dailyObjectives: Ngày 7: Bước 1 – Nhận biết I, my, mine trong câu về công việc của bản thân.
Ngày 8: Bước 1 – Nhận biết he, him, his và they, them, their trong tin nhắn nhóm.

steps.focus: Sở hữu cách 's và câu hỏi Whose…?
steps.usage: Dùng 's với tên người hoặc danh từ chỉ người để nói sở hữu (Anna's desk). Dùng Whose…? để hỏi vật thuộc về ai, và mine/his/theirs để trả lời mà không cần lặp lại danh từ.
steps.formula: Whose + danh từ + is this? / Anna's + danh từ; danh từ + 's / mine / his / theirs
examples: Whose laptop is this? It's mine.
Anna's desk is near the window.
The budget file is his, not hers.
dailyObjectives: Ngày 9: Bước 2 – Dùng sở hữu cách 's với tên người (Anna's desk).
Ngày 10: Bước 2 – Đặt câu hỏi Whose…? và trả lời bằng mine, his, theirs.

steps.focus: Lỗi thường gặp với đại từ và sở hữu
steps.usage: Lỗi phổ biến: dùng me làm chủ ngữ (Me am), dùng my và mine sai chỗ, quên 's hoặc dùng sai hình thức sở hữu. Tiếng Việt không có đại từ sở hữu tương tự nên cần chú ý trật tự.
steps.formula: Subject pronoun + verb; possessive adjective + noun; Whose + noun + is/are…?
examples: Wrong: Me is the team leader. → Right: I am the team leader.
Wrong: This is mine desk. → Right: This is my desk.
Wrong: Whose is this file? It is Tom file. → Right: Whose file is this? It's Tom's file.
dailyObjectives: Ngày 11: Bước 3 – Sửa lỗi dùng me làm chủ ngữ và nhầm my với mine.
Ngày 12: Bước 3 – Viết 1–2 câu về đồ dùng và phần việc của mình với my, his, their và 's.

steps.focus: Stative verbs in continuous form for emphasis; simple present for summaries and storytelling
steps.usage: Stative verbs such as love, want and need are normally used in simple tenses. In continuous form they show strong or temporary feeling. The simple present is also used to summarise a report or to tell the story of a document or meeting.
steps.formula: Subject + am/is/are + stative verb (love, hate, want, need) + object  |  Subject + present simple verb + ... (summary)
examples: I'm loving the new dashboard. It saves our team two hours a week.
The report shows that sales rise in the third quarter, and the team meets its target.
We're needing more time for the vendor review, so I'm proposing a new date.
dailyObjectives: Day 1 (Step 1 – Identify): Notice the continuous form of a stative verb for emphasis (I'm loving…) and the simple present used to summarise a report.
Day 2 (Step 1 – Basic structure): Build the core pattern subject + am/is/are + stative verb, and the simple present summary pattern subject + present verb in a workplace update.

steps.focus: Continuous forms for polite requests; present perfect continuous for lasting traces
steps.usage: Use the past continuous with was wondering to make a request softer and more polite in a meeting. Use the present perfect continuous to describe an activity that has left a visible result now, such as tired eyes or a messy file.
steps.formula: I was wondering if + subject + could/would + verb  |  Subject + have/has been + -ing (+ result still visible)
examples: I was wondering if we could move the planning session to Thursday.
The team has been working on the migration all week, so the test environment is still unstable.
Our client has been asking for a revised quote, and that is why the budget file looks different.
dailyObjectives: Day 3 (Step 2 – Variations): Practise the negative and question variants of I was wondering if… and the question form of the continuous for polite requests.
Day 4 (Step 2 – Meaning and use): Learn when the present perfect continuous shows a trace or visible result (has been + -ing) and signal words such as all week, lately and recently.

steps.focus: Avoiding Vietnamese-influenced tense errors; past perfect versus past simple when order is clear
steps.usage: Vietnamese has no tense marking, so learners often forget the -ed ending, the auxiliary, or mix past simple and past perfect. Use the past perfect only when two past events need an order; when the order is obvious from context, the past simple is enough and sounds natural.
steps.formula: Had + past participle (earlier action) + ... + past simple (later action)  |  Past simple alone when the order is already clear
examples: By the time the client called, we had already fixed the bug.
We fixed the bug before the client called.
When I joined the project, the design team had finished the prototype.
dailyObjectives: Day 5 (Step 3 – Common errors): Correct common Vietnamese-influenced errors: missing -ed, missing auxiliary, and wrong tense when there is no tense marker in Vietnamese.
Day 6 (Step 3 – Application): Write one or two sentences about your own year-end work, using continuous emphasis, polite continuous requests or past perfect where the order matters.

steps.focus: Be to for formal schedules; be about to and be on the point of for imminent action
steps.usage: Be to is used for official arrangements, instructions or schedules from management. Be about to and be on the point of describe an action that is going to happen in the very near future, often within minutes.
steps.formula: Subject + am/is/are + to + base verb (official plan)  |  Subject + am/is/are about to / on the point of + base verb (very soon)
examples: The steering committee is to review the year-end budget on 15 December.
We are about to send the revised roadmap to the client.
The product lead is on the point of announcing the new release date.
dailyObjectives: Day 1 (Step 1 – Identify): Notice be to in an official schedule notice and be about to in a short workplace update.
Day 2 (Step 1 – Basic structure): Build the affirmative forms of be to and be about to / be on the point of with a base verb.

steps.focus: Be due to and be bound/likely to for expected events; future in the past
steps.usage: Be due to refers to a planned or scheduled event, often with a deadline. Be bound to and be likely to describe strong expectation. In the past, use was going to, was to have, and would for plans that were made earlier but may have changed.
steps.formula: Subject + am/is/are due to + base verb  |  Subject + is/are bound/likely to + base verb  |  Subject + was/were going to / was/were to have / would + base verb (past plan)
examples: The annual review is due to start on 10 December, so please prepare your slides.
Our team is likely to finish the migration before the holiday break.
We were going to present the results last week, but the client asked for a delay.
dailyObjectives: Day 3 (Step 2 – Variations): Practise negatives and questions with be due to, and the negative form of be likely to (is not likely to).
Day 4 (Step 2 – Meaning and use): Learn the difference between be due to, be bound to and be likely to, and use future in the past with was going to, was to have and would.

steps.focus: Avoiding Vietnamese-influenced future errors; choosing the right future form
steps.usage: Vietnamese speakers often forget the to after be, add -ing, or use will where an official or scheduled form is better. Choose be to for official plans, be due to for scheduled deadlines, and be about to for immediate action.
steps.formula: Be + to/about to/due to + base verb (not: be to + -ing / to + -ing)  |  Would + base verb is for the past, not for a fixed future plan
examples: The board is to approve the budget on Friday. (not: is to approving)
The release is due to go live next month. (not: is due go live)
When I joined, I thought the team would hire two more engineers, but the plan changed.
dailyObjectives: Day 5 (Step 3 – Common errors): Correct errors such as missing to after be, adding -ing after to, and using would for a future plan that is still open.
Day 6 (Step 3 – Application): Write one or two sentences about a plan or deadline for next year, using be to, be due to or be likely to.

content.text: Notice the continuous form of a stative verb for emphasis (I'm loving…) and the simple present used to summarise a report.
items: Evaluate a project report in a team meeting.
Summarise meeting minutes for a manager.
Suggest ways to mitigate a delivery risk.

content.text: Read the examples, notice the grammar pattern, then answer the short tasks. Focus on how the verb form changes the meaning.
steps: Read each example sentence aloud once.
Notice which verb is in the continuous form and which verb is in the simple present.
Answer the grammar questions and check the explanation after each one.

items.meaning: đánh giá (một cách có hệ thống)

antonyms.definition: fail to notice or consider something
list of topics planned for a meeting

umbrella.meaning: tài liệu ghi chép bằng văn bản

items.meaning: giảm nhẹ, làm giảm bớt (rủi ro, vấn đề)

antonyms.definition: make a problem become more serious
make a bad situation even worse

content.text: Verbs like love, want and need are usually simple. With am/is/are they show strong or temporary feeling. The simple present can also summarise a report.

items.answer: I'm loving the new reporting tool our team is using.
items.prompt: Which sentence uses a stative verb in the continuous form for emphasis?
options: We need a larger budget for the project.
I'm loving the new reporting tool our team is using.
The minutes record the decision of the board.
They evaluate the results every quarter.
items.explanation: 'Loving' is a stative verb in the continuous form, showing strong feeling. The other sentences use simple tenses.

items.answer: The report shows that costs fall in the second half of the year.
items.prompt: Which sentence uses the simple present to summarise a report?
options: The report is showing that costs are falling.
The report has been showing costs fall.
The report shows that costs fall in the second half of the year.
The report was shows that costs fall.
items.explanation: The simple present 'shows' summarises what the report says, which is the function being noticed today.

items.answer: We approved the minutes of last week's meeting.
items.prompt: Which sentence uses 'minutes' correctly in a workplace context?
options: We are minuting the weather for the holiday.
The minutes is very heavy on the table.
We approved the minutes of last week's meeting.
items.explanation: 'Minutes' here means the written record of a meeting, and it is used with approve or circulate.

items.answer: We will mitigate the risk by adding a backup plan.
items.prompt: Which sentence uses 'mitigate' with the correct meaning?
options: We will mitigate the risk by adding a backup plan.
We will mitigate the new office on Monday.
We mitigate our team lunch every Friday.
They mitigate the meeting room for the guests.
items.explanation: 'Mitigate' means to reduce the seriousness of a problem or risk, so it fits with 'risk'.

content.formula: Subject + am/is/are + stative verb (love, hate, want, need) + object  |  Subject + present simple verb + ... (summary)
examples: I'm loving the new dashboard that the team built for us.
The minutes show that the group agreed to evaluate the vendor contract before March.
We're needing more time to mitigate the delay, so I'm proposing a new schedule.
content.objective: Day 1 (Step 1 – Identify): Notice the continuous form of a stative verb for emphasis (I'm loving…) and the simple present used to summarise a report.
Hear, identify and produce the target sound or feature; repeat three words after a model

content.prompt: What did the team agree to do in the last session?
content.script: Good morning, everyone. Thanks for joining the year-end review. Before we start, I'd like to share the minutes from our last session. The team agreed to evaluate the new vendor contract, and we also discussed how to mitigate the delay in the testing phase. Right now, I'm loving the progress on the dashboard, because it saves each member about two hours a week. Let's begin with the results.

content.text:
Subject: Q4 Progress Update

Hi team,

The minutes from our October meeting are now attached. The report shows that the support queue is shorter than last quarter, and the team meets its response target most days. We plan to evaluate the new ticketing tool in January. To mitigate the risk of staff overload during the holiday period, we will add a temporary rota. Please review the work document before Friday and send any questions to me.

Thanks,
Linh
